evidence.quote: LA 66 winds through the scenic Tunica Hills of West Feliciana Parish and connects the prison facility with US 61, the main highway through the area.

evidence.claim: LA 66 winds through the wooded Tunica Hills, a two-lane road running 19.62 miles from the Angola prison entrance to US 61 north of St. Francisville.
evidence.quote: It runs 19.62 miles (31.58 km) in a general east–west direction from the main entrance of the Louisiana State Penitentiary at Angola to a junction with U.S. Highway 61 (US 61) north of St. Francisville.

evidence.claim: The entire highway belongs to the Louisiana Scenic Byways system as the Tunica Trace Byway.
evidence.quote: The entire route of LA 66 is known as the Tunica Trace Byway in the state-designated system of tourist routes known as the Louisiana Scenic Byways.

evidence.claim: Some sharper curves have been straightened by cuts into the hills; at Tunica, one bypassed bend survives as Crescent Road.
evidence.quote: Since then, the route has remained unchanged apart from reconstruction projects over the years which have straightened some of its sharper curves by cutting into the terrain.  This is especially evident in Tunica, where a bypassed curve still exists as Crescent Road,

evidence.claim: The route derives from a Native American portage known as the Tunica Trace.
evidence.quote: the route is derived from an ancient Native American portage known as the Tunica Trace.

evidence.claim: In 1926, the legislature added State Route 124, creating a state-maintained connection between Angola and the main highway through the area.
evidence.quote: The addition of Route 124 created a state-maintained access road from the prison to the main highway through the area, State Route 3,

evidence.claim: The dirt road received gravel by 1929 and pavement in 1939, then became LA 66 in the 1955 renumbering.
evidence.quote: Route 124 was an unimproved dirt road when originally designated in 1926.  The entire route was gravel surfaced by 1929 and then paved a decade later, in 1939.

evidence.claim: The state legislature designated the scenic byway in 1988, and West Feliciana Parish changed its local name from Angola Road to Tunica Trace to emphasize that history.
evidence.quote: In 1988, the entire route of LA 66 was designated by the state legislature as the Tunica Trace Scenic Byway within the Louisiana Scenic Byways program.

evidence.claim: Driving east from the prison gate, the road passes through Tunica and curves northeast between the wildlife management area’s two tracts.
evidence.quote: LA 66 heads southeast through a thickly wooded rural area and passes through the tiny community of Tunica.  The highway then curves to the northeast, passing between the north and south tracts of the Tunica Hills Wildlife Management Area.

evidence.claim: At Retreat it turns southeast, continuing through Turnbull and Weyanoke.
evidence.quote: After reaching a point about one mile (1.6 km) from the state line in an area known as Retreat, LA 66 curves back to the southeast

evidence.claim: The final stretch roughly follows the east side of Little Bayou Sara, crosses Big Bayou Sara on a 1940s pony truss bridge, and reaches US 61 at Bains.
evidence.quote: LA 66 continues for another 6.4 miles (10.3 km), roughly following the east side of the serpentine Little Bayou Sara. It then bends eastward to cross the main branch of Bayou Sara, also known as Big Bayou Sara, by way of a pony truss bridge dating to the 1940s.  LA 66 proceeds a short distance further to a junction with US 61 in the community of Bains.

evidence.claim: The prison occupies land assembled as four plantations by slave trader Isaac Franklin in the 1830s.

evidence.claim: His widow sold them to Samuel Lawrence James in 1880.

evidence.quote: Under the convict lease system, Major James ran his vast plantation using convicts leased from the state as his workers.
